summary: This paper introduces path–endpoint separation pulses (PESP), which decouple control of transient leakage exposure (time-integrated population in noncomputational states) from residual endpoint leakage in fast transmon gates. Using a spectral argument, the authors show that endpoint leakage depends on drive spectral weight at the anharmonicity $\eta$, while transient exposure depends on spectral weight over a frequency band of width $\sim 1/T$, making them independently controllable.
motivation: Leakage to noncomputational states limits gate speed in weakly anharmonic transmons, but conventional methods like DRAG suppress only endpoint leakage. Since pure dephasing converts transient exposure into residual leakage even when closed-system evolution returns to the computational subspace, minimizing endpoint amplitude alone does not reduce noise-induced leakage.
method: PESP combines a path-shaping pulse (PSP) that minimizes time-averaged leakage exposure $\bar{P}_A$ via a cosine-basis envelope with coefficients $a_2, a_3$ and generalized DRAG, followed by an endpoint-cancellation pulse (ECP) with two tones near $-\eta$ and $-2\eta$ to suppress residual $|2\rangle$ and $|3\rangle$ populations. Optimization uses staged cost functions via CMA-ES, with the operating point selected at the four-level leakage-floor knee.
result: For a 10 ns $R_X(\pi/2)$ gate at $\eta/2\pi = 0.2$ GHz, the PSP reduces dephasing-induced exposure by 21% relative to cosine DRAG, confirmed by independent Lindblad simulations showing 20% reduction in excess leakage. The two-tone ECP lowers coherent endpoint leakage from $7\times10^{-7}$ to $3\times10^{-8}$ without increasing transient exposure, whereas matched-budget endpoint-only and FAST DRAG baselines produce no path reduction despite lower endpoint floors.
